{"id": "96:2/q14", "question": "What was first revealed, and how much of this sura came first?", "turns_on": "Whether 'first sura' means the opening five verses or the complete chapter, and the competing priority claims.", "positions": [{"id": "96:2/q14/p1", "position": "The opening five verses of al-ʿAlaq, ending at 96:5, were the first revelation; the remainder came later.", "reasons": "Tabari preserves Aisha, Ubayd b. Umayr, Abu Raja, Ata and Mujahid, the latter adding Nun and the Pen afterward. Wahidi reports some scholars locating the five at Hira. Baghawi and Thalabi cite most commentators. Ibn Kathir calls these the first mercy. Burhan says Bukhari's Aisha report was authenticated by al-Hakim and Muslim extends to 96:5. Durr cites Ibn Abbas. Ibn Ashur bases the conclusion on Aisha, Abu Musa and most exegetes and dates it Ramadan 17, year 40 after the Elephant. Bint al-Shati says Tabari and biography stop at verse five and cites Razi for later completion amid opposition; she reports Abu Hayyan judging Muddaththir and Fatiha first claims unsound."}, {"id": "96:2/q14/p2", "position": "Al-ʿAlaq is described as the first sura revealed, without necessarily fixing the extent of the first installment.", "reasons": "Tabari transmits Aisha, Abu Raja, Ata, Mujahid and Ubayd's formulations of 'first sura'; Jishumi relays Aisha, Mujahid and Ata. Itqan relays Ubayd's first-sura claim."}, {"id": "96:2/q14/p3", "position": "Al-Muddaththir or al-Fatiha came first.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shati reports Abu Hayyan's judgment that these alternative priority claims are unsound."}]}

{"id": "96:2/q18", "question": "How does this verse connect with neighboring suras and the rest of al-ʿAlaq?", "turns_on": "The sources link the verse to earlier suras through human origin and destiny, prophetic rank, or the reported chest opening.", "positions": [{"id": "96:2/q18/p1", "position": "Al-Tin's best human form is followed by al-ʿAlaq's account of human material origin and later destiny.", "reasons": "Alusi links 95:4 to the material origin and afterlife. The Qur'an's guidance explains beginnings and ends, and sūra order is based on arrangement, not revelation chronology."}, {"id": "96:2/q18/p2", "position": "The preceding suras show the Prophet's highest rank, while this sura also portrays a person who forbids prayer.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Zubayr compares promised satisfaction and expanded breast, 93:5 and 94:1, with Moses' prayer at 20:25; he contrasts the blocker of prayer in 96:9 with the command to disobey him in 96:19."}, {"id": "96:2/q18/p3", "position": "The clot's creation and the return to God frame the sura's story of accountability.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shati links human origin to 92:13 and says the first revelation sketches the human story later expanded in passages on resurrection and judgment. {"id": "96:2/q19", "question": "What wider Quranic themes are anticipated by the opening passage?", "turns_on": "Whether the opening is related to wider creation and accountability passages or to letters, writing and the Quranic challenge.", "positions": [{"id": "96:2/q19/p1", "position": "Its reading command and creation, pen and teaching themes preview the Quran's guidance and human accountability.", "reasons": "Itqan calls the opening a title of the Qur'an because it names reading in God's name, legal and religious knowledge, and divine teaching. {"id": "96:3/q01", "question": "Why is the command to read repeated?", "turns_on": "Whether the repetition is emphasis, distinguishes audiences or settings, or directly answers the Prophet's inability to read.", "positions": [{"id": "96:3/q01/p1", "position": "The second command reinforces the first, stresses reading, and prepares the declaration of divine generosity.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī says repetition establishes certainty; al-Baghawī, Ibn al-Jawzī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Ālūsī, Ibn ʿĀshūr, al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī, and Bint al-Shāṭiʾ describe emphasis. Rāzī and al-Ālūsī also transmit an unrestricted first reading; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī rejects the private/public distinction as unsupported by the wording. Al-Wāḥidī's and Elmalılı's accounts of reciting for others overlap this purpose."}, {"id": "96:3/q01/p3", "position": "The first command is to learn from Gabriel and the second to teach.", "reasons": "Rāzī gives learning then teaching as one distinction; Bint al-Shāṭiʾ records it from earlier exegetes."}, {"id": "96:3/q01/p4", "position": "The two commands distinguish recitation in prayer from recitation outside prayer.", "reasons": "Rāzī and Bint al-Shāṭiʾ

{"id": "96:3/q02", "question": "What is the Prophet commanded to read, and how does the command relate to God's name?", "turns_on": "The omitted object of 'read' and which verb receives the name phrase; adjacency is al-Ālūsī's stated syntactic test.", "positions": [{"id": "96:3/q02/p1", "position": "He is to read the revelation or Qur'an given to him, beginning in his Lord's name.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās supplies the omitted object 'what was revealed to you' and says God will not withhold its reward. Al-Jishumī names the Qur'an. Al-Ālūsī and Qatādah say to begin with God's name; Qatādah says omitting the basmala or using an idol's name would fail the command. Al-Ālūsī prefers attaching 'in your Lord's name' to the adjacent first verb: placing the verb first foregrounds recitation in the opening sūra, while fronting the name would presuppose reading. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ says revelation then specifies what is recited."}, {"id": "96:3/q02/p2", "position": "The first command concerns God's name and the second the Qur'an.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī reports this alternative, distinguishing the content of the two commands."}, {"id": "96:3/q02/p3", "position": "The name phrase attaches to the second command, while the first establishes recitation itself.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports an analysis that gives 'in God's name' its customary attachment, makes the first recite introduce reading, and connects 'in your Lord's name' with the second command. Its proponents answer that the first command already orders recitation."}, {"id": "96:3/q02/p4", "position": "The basmala's 'in the name' attaches to the first command and 'in your Lord's name' to the second, specifying the opening name.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī calls this remote, since the name phrase normally attaches to the adjacent verb."}]}
{"id": "96:3/q03", "question": "How is 'your Lord is the Most Generous' constructed?", "turns_on": "Whether the Lord clause stands independently or circumstantially, and whether al-akram or the following relative clause is its predicate.", "positions": [{"id": "96:3/q03/p1", "position": "It is an independent new sentence, with 'your Lord' as subject and 'the Most Generous' as predicate.", "reasons": "Al-Baghawī, Ibn al-Jawzī, al-Qurṭubī, Bursevī, and al-Ālūsī place a sentence break after the command. Bursevī permits a pause after khalaq because Muhammad said he could not read. Ibn ʿĀshūr calls it an explanatory answer to that concern. Corpus Coranicum notes parallels at 89:15, 82:6, and 55:27, and says Paret's examples at 6:133 and 18:58 can support a definite elative predicate."}, {"id": "96:3/q03/p2", "position": "The Lord clause is circumstantial to the implied subject of 'read': read while your Lord is most generous.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī says this highlights the Prophet's benefactor; al-Ālūsī reports it as an alternative that can remove the literacy objection."}, {"id": "96:3/q03/p3", "position": "Al-Akram is an adjective of 'your Lord'; the following relative clause supplies the predicate.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Shaykh explicitly parses rabbuka as subject, al-akram as adjective and the relative clause as predicate. Corpus Coranicum reports Paret's preference for this reading. Elmalılı says this better fits the context and puts prophetic honor above the pen's honor; either definite-predicate order suggests exclusivity."}, {"id": "96:3/q03/p4", "position": "Al-Akram is the predicate, and the following relative clause is an adjective.", "reasons": "Elmalılı gives this alternate parsing; he says its definite predicate also conveys exclusivity."}]}
{"id": "96:3/q04", "question": "Why say 'your Lord' here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "96:3/q04/p1", "position": "The title stresses God's care for Muhammad and recalls the command to read in His name.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says rabbuka replaces the expected pronoun to emphasize divine care and to connect the Lord-title with the earlier command. {"id": "96:3/q05", "question": "What does 'al-Akram' mean here?", "turns_on": "The semantic scope of generosity and whether the definite elative compares God with givers or denotes unrestricted supremacy.", "positions": [{"id": "96:3/q05/p1", "position": "God is generous beyond every giver, the source of gifts that no other can originate.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī and al-Qushayrī give the ordinary sense 'generous'; al-Qurṭubī prefers it because preceding favors prove generosity. Al-Khaṭṭābī allows an elative equal to the positive. Al-Jishumī and al-Ṭabrisī say God initiates every blessing, directly or by its means. Al-Zamakhsharī, al-Nasafī, Abū Ḥayyān, al-Bayḍāwī and others cite countless gifts, forbearance, repentance and forgiveness. Ibrāhīm al-Yashkurī says God feeds a servant who worships another. Rāzī adduces a poem on increased kindness after offense and distinguishes divine gifts from human gifts sought for praise, reward or protection. Ibn ʿĀshūr defines karam as giving beneficial gifts, including existence and sustenance. Study Quran says Qur'anic application of karīm to God introduced a new divine attribute to pagan Arabs. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ objects to restricting the definite unqualified form to finite comparison."}, {"id": "96:3/q05/p2", "position": "Al-Akram expresses God's absolute, unbounded generosity and perfection, without specifying another giver for comparison.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr treats the form as intensity rather than comparison; al-Biqāʿī includes perfection of essence, attributes and acts without defect. Elmalılı calls gifts limitless and gratuitous. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ argues that definite, unqualified afʿal and fuʿlā express an unrestricted maximum, citing 87:1, 92:20 and images of the greatest sign, blow, calamity, fire and model; explicit min or a named object limits a true comparison, as in 2:191. She contrasts 49:13's human scope and the genuinely comparative 'best of plotters' in 27:50 and 3:54; she rejects an argument that 'the Highest' implies a lesser lord and rejects explaining the form as rhyme. Her Quranic survey uses karīm for God, throne, messenger, angel, scripture and rewards, and notes ironic 'mighty, noble' at 44:47."}, {"id": "96:3/q05/p3", "position": "Al-Akram means the Forbearing, who overlooks ignorance and does not hasten punishment.", "reasons": "Al-Kalbī's gloss is relayed by al-Thaʿlabī, al-Wāḥidī, al-Baghawī and al-Qurṭubī; al-Wāḥidī adds wisdom. Al-Jishumī reports the same sense. Al-Qurṭubī also reports 'overlooks servants' ignorance' without explicit mention of delayed punishment."}, {"id": "96:3/q05/p4", "position": "The root carries nobility and honor, opposed to baseness or humiliation.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shāṭiʾ distinguishes karam from baseness and ikrām from humiliation, citing God's honoring or humiliating people at 22:18 and 49:13. Study Quran says pre-Islamic karāmah included lineage, character and magnanimity."}]}

{"id": "96:3/q08", "question": "What do the opening verses establish about God and human obligation?", "turns_on": "The notes move from proof by creation and teaching to claims about divine action; al-Qāshānī supplies an inward reading.", "positions": [{"id": "96:3/q08/p1", "position": "Creation and teaching prove a knowing, wise, powerful, merciful Lord, whom people should know and worship.", "reasons": "Rāzī says creation from a clot rationally proves power, wisdom, knowledge and mercy; life's change into knowledge discloses direction and determination. Al-Bayḍāwī calls knowing God the first obligation and says the opening first points to His existence, power and wisdom. Al-Jishumī says the creator and master benefits others, hence deserves worship. Ibn ʿĀshūr says lordship entails existence and oneness, creation and teaching indicate acts, and al-Akram conveys perfection and freedom from deficiency."}, {"id": "96:3/q08/p2", "position": "Divine generosity cannot aim at a gain or require compensation; God does not impose beyond capacity or without reward.", "reasons": "Rāzī defines generosity as fitting benefit without recompense, counting praise, reward and escaping blame as returns. {"id": "96:3/q11", "question": "What happened after the first encounter at Hira?", "turns_on": "These reports supply different episodes and sequence details after the first encounter.", "positions": [{"id": "96:3/q11/p1", "position": "Khadijah reassured the frightened Prophet by his virtues, and Waraqa identified Gabriel as Moses' angel and foresaw opposition.", "reasons": "Reports list kinship, truthfulness, bearing burdens, feeding or helping the needy, hospitality and aid in hardship, with small variations. {"id": "96:3/q12", "question": "Which part of this sura was revealed first?", "turns_on": "Whether 'first sura' fixes the entire sura's timing or the five-verse opening; several reports explicitly stop at verse five.", "positions": [{"id": "96:3/q12/p1", "position": "The opening five verses, through 'what he did not know,' came first at Hira; the rest came later.", "reasons": "ʿĀʾishah's first encounter and Ibn ʿAbbās's account end at verse five. Al-Burhān says al-Ḥākim authenticated ʿĀʾishah's Bukhārī report and Muslim gives it through 96:5.
